newsitem.title: ANGOLA: UN unimpressed by UNITA bid to avoid sanctions.
newsitem.headline: UN unimpressed by UNITA bid to avoid sanctions.

text.p: The United Nations on Thursday branded as incomplete proposals by Angola's former rebel movement UNITA to revive a stalled peace process, but said a final decision on whether to implement sanctions would come later.

The U.N. Security Council warned it would impose sanctions including travel and banking restrictions from Friday unless UNITA took steps to comply with the 1994 peace accord which ended two decades of civil war against the formerly Marxist government of President Jose Eduardo dos Santos. UNITA responded this week.

"After a deep analysis of the information presented, the (U.N. Observer Mission in Angola) and the (observer nations) found that UNITA did not respond in a concrete way to ... the Security Council resolution of June 30, 1997," the U.N. mission said in a statement.
The statement said the number of men that UNITA claimed to have under arms was "highly incomplete" and the information the former rebels had offered on arms was "insufficient".
David Wimhurst, spokesman for the U.N. mission, had initially said the U.N. decision would be announced by the Joint Commission, the body overseeing the peace process in Angola.
Officials said later, however, the decision whether to impose sanctions against UNITA probably would be announced in New York.
Wimhurst said the UNITA proposals addressed three key demands made by the Security Council on June 30 to avert sanctions.

The demands included handing over the vast amount of territory UNITA still controls to the government, defining the number of armed men it still controls and turning its propaganda short-wave radio station, Vorgan, into a non-partisan entity.

A source involved in the peace process said UNITA had agreed to transform its radio station after a feasibility study, but that areas UNITA was proposing to hand over were remote and surrounded by other UNITA-held territory.
The Security Council gave UNITA until August 15 to submit a plan of how to move forward on the three demands.

On Tuesday, Security Council President Sir John Weston turned up the pressure, saying: "We will consider and we will impose additional measures. Let no one say later that they were not warned. The situation is totally unacceptable."
The European Union urged UNITA on Thursday to comply.
UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, fought the government from 1975 until the two sides signed a peace agreement in the Zambian capital Lusaka in 1994.

Under the terms of the treaty the former rebels were to disarm completely and hand their territory -- whose diamond mines provide the movement led by Jonas Savimbi with a hefty income -- to the government.

But UNITA still controls up to 70 percent of Angola and the government says UNITA still has 35,000 armed troops. Military analysts and diplomats in Luanda estimate UNITA troop strength at between 15,000 and 25,000.
UNITA claims in a new document seen by Retuers to have 5,448 armed men -- almost twice as many as previously admitted.
